apidocs/SystemLibrary.Common.Framework.A.summary: Namespace SystemLibrary.Common.Framework.App Client is a class for all http(s) requests in your project Uses HttpClient and Polly behind the scenes for features such as reusing tcp connections, retry on 502 and 504 status codes, and optionally a request breaker for 7 seconds, if 25 error codes (404, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 505) occurs in a row useRetryPolicy: false, will retry once if request is a file request or GET or POST and status code is 502 or 504 Options: useRetryPolicy: True: same as 'false', but adds: retries one additional time on 502, 504 GET, POST - retries up to two times if response is null (timeout/no response) retries once on 401 GET, POST - retries once on 404 GET retries once on 500 GET, POST - retries once on 404, 500, 502 504 file request retries once on OPTION, PATCH, HEAD, CONNECT, TRACE ▼ Example ✕ You can simply "var client = new Client()" if you want and use the methods directly or inherit it and base all your integrations on it, sharing headers or other methods you would like. A simple class and HttpBinClient: class HttpBinResponse { public string Url { get; set; } } class HttpBinClient : Client { const string apiUrl = "http://httpbin.org"; public HttpBinClient() : base(useRetryPolicy: true) { } public HttpBinResponse Get() { return base.Get<HttpBinResponse>(apiUrl + "/get").Data; } } Running the above Client and Response in a UnitTest project as such: [TestMethod] public void Test() { var client = new HttpBinClient(); var response = client.Get(); Assert.IsTrue(response.Url.Contains("http")); //Visit: http://httpbin.org/get to see the actual value of 'url', then you know this Assert statement is true } Another example of using the Client directly: public void Test() { var client = new Client(); var response = client.Get<string>("http://httpbin.org/get"); Assert.IsTrue(response.Contains("http")); //Response is now the whole json (or any data actually as a string) text that the url: http://httpbin.org/get is returning } Another example returning HttpResponseMessage as is, for you to read the stream/content of the response yourself: public void Test() { var client = new Client(); var response = = client.Get<HttpResponseMessage>("http://httpbin.org/get"); var httpResponseMessage = response.Data; // httpResponseMessage now is ready to be read if you need to read it manually, as in: it's not a json/xml/serialization type of response, but maybe an Stream/Image you need to read... } ▼ Remarks ✕ Every client uses the Default configurations, which you can override in appsettings.json Most default configurations can again be overriden in the Clients constructor Each HttpClient pool behind the scenes, is based on scheme, url, port and timeout Each method also take an additional timeout parameter, a different timeout will target a different HttpClient Each underlying HttpClient is used for default 20 minutes, each TCP connection is maximum reused for 4 minutes and 55 seconds A 502 or 504 response on GET, POST or file request will always be retried once, cannot be turned off unless RetryTimeout is set to 0 in appSettings A new client wont neccesary create a new HttpClient, it might use from cache, it all depends on the url and params you pass in - In theory you could create just one client reusing towards any url you want But it's now up to you now: You want a new instance? documentation/apifilters.html.title: Api Filters | System Library Common Framework
documentation/apifilters.html.summary: Api Filters Attribute-based request filters for access control on controllers and actions. Built on top of BaseApiFilterAttribute which provides flexible value matching via exact string, wildcard, pipe-delimited or regex patterns. Features ApiTokenFilter: validates the api-token request header (or custom header name) OriginFilter: validates the Origin request header UserAgentFilter: validates the User-Agent request header — also blocks known bots, crawlers and spiders automatically when applied BaseApiFilterAttribute: base class for building custom filter attributes with built-in header value matching Behavior All filters use the same matching logic inherited from BaseApiFilterAttribute, evaluated in this order: null or * → allows all Exact string → case-sensitive match Pipe-delimited a|b → case-insensitive contains match against any part Wildcard *text* → case-insensitive starts/ends/contains match Regex ^pattern$ → compiled with RegexOptions.IgnoreCase — always case-insensitive On access denied, returns HTTP 403 with a JSON error body. Caveats Regex matching silently falls back to no-match if the pattern is invalid — no exception is thrown ApiTokenFilter defaults to api-token header name but accepts any custom header name UserAgentFilter blocks known bots and crawlers regardless of the match pattern — adding the attribute always enables bot blocking Filters return application/json on access denied — plain text and XML responses not yet supported Tip Inherit BaseApiFilterAttribute to build your own filter attributes — override OnActionExecuting and use RequestHasValidHeaderValue and OnAccessDenied for consistent behavior. Multiple attributes on the same controller are AND'd — every filter must pass. Use pipe-delimited values for OR logic, for instance: [ApiTokenFilter("token1|token2|token3")] Examples [ApiTokenFilter("SecretToken")] [OriginFilter("*.systemlibrary.com")] [UserAgentFilter("Chrome|Edg|Firefox")] public class OrderController : BaseApiController { } [ApiTokenFilter("^DEV-[A-Z0-9]{6}$")] public ActionResult SensitiveEndpoint() { }

documentation/application.html.title: Application | System Library Common Framework
documentation/application.html.summary: Application Entry point for starting and stopping the framework host. The class wraps ASP.NET host creation and exposes several startup patterns depending on how much control you need. Features Startup helpers: Start, StartAsync, Build, and host shutdown helpers Hook lifecycle: IFrameworkHooks callbacks during host construction and startup Async support: sync and async startup/shutdown variants Flexible startup: either framework-managed startup or direct host-builder configuration Behavior Start API The simplest pattern is to let the framework create and run the host for you: var options = new FrameworkOptions(); Application.Start<Hooks>(AppType.Web, options, AppHosting.Kestrel); public class Hooks : IFrameworkHooks { public void OnConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services, EnvironmentType env) { } } This registers the framework services and middleware, builds the host, and blocks until shutdown. Build API Use the build helper when you want to configure the host builder before running it: var options = new FrameworkOptions(); var urls = new[] { "http://localhost:5010" }; var builder = Application.Build<Hooks>(AppType.Web, options, AppHosting.Kestrel, urls); var app = builder.Build(); app.Run(); Extension API Full control via extension methods directly on the host builder. IFrameworkHooks is not invoked in this mode. This is the pattern the repo uses in its current demo application: var builder = Host.CreateDefaultBuilder(args); builder.ConfigureFrameworkLogging(); builder.ConfigureServices((context, services) => { services = services.AddFrameworkServices(AppType.Web, options); }); builder = builder.ConfigureWebHostDefaults(webBuilder => { webBuilder.ConfigureFrameworkHosting(); webBuilder.Configure(app => { app.UseFrameworkBeginMiddlewares(AppType.Web); app.UseFrameworkEndMiddlewares(AppType.Web); }); }); var app = builder.Build(); app.Run(); This approach gives the application full control over the host and pipeline while still using the framework's service registrations and middleware extensions. Stopping the host Application.HostStop(); // or await Application.HostStopAsync(); Caveats Calling Start or StartAsync twice throws InvalidOperationException because only one host instance is allowed at a time. The IFrameworkHooks lifecycle is skipped when the extension API is used directly. For most applications, the HostBuilder + AddFrameworkServices pattern is the clearest and most explicit option. Tip Use Application.Start when you want the framework to manage the host lifecycle. Use Application.Build when you need to configure the host before Run(). Use the extension API when you already have an ASP.NET host setup and want direct control over the pipeline.

documentation/basetest.html.title: BaseTest | System Library Common Framework
documentation/basetest.html.summary: BaseTest BaseTest provides shared assertion helpers and test utilities for MSTest projects. It also provides the base class for the framework's ASP.NET integration test helpers. Features Test lifecycle: Provides MSTest cleanup and flushes pending framework logs once. Assertions: Includes IsOk, IsEmpty, IsNull, IsException, and other assertion helpers. Polling: When() waits for a condition to become true. Test context: Exposes MSTest's TestContext. Behavior TestCleanup() flushes pending logs during the first cleanup and waits briefly for background tasks to finish. When() checks the condition immediately, then retries every 50ms for up to approximately 10 seconds. Exceptions thrown by the condition are ignored while waiting. Assertion failures throw exceptions. Example public class MyTests : BaseTest { [TestMethod] public void TestSomething() { var result = service.GetValue(); IsOk(result); IsNull(null); IsEmpty(""); IsException(() => service.DoSomethingInvalid()); } } Caveats IsEmpty() checks for an empty string, not empty collections. IsException() only verifies that an exception was thrown; it does not check its type. When() returns false when the condition does not become true within the timeout.

documentation/basetestkestrel.html.title: BaseTestKestrel | System Library Common Framework
documentation/basetestkestrel.html.summary: BaseTestKestrel BaseTestKestrel provides an ASP.NET Core test host using a real local web server. It supports testing framework actions and controller routes through HTTP requests. Features Local hosting: Starts a WebApplication on a configured local port. Action mapping: Maps public methods ending in __Action to HTTP endpoints. Controller testing: Supports requests to arbitrary application routes. Custom configuration: Supports callbacks for services, application configuration, and logging. HTTP helpers: Provides helpers for action-based requests and controller routes. Host reuse: Reuses the running application for tests sharing the same port. Behavior The host is initialized lazily when Client is first accessed. HostStart() triggers this initialization. Each port identifies one shared WebApplication instance. Derived test classes using the same port therefore share the same host. Public methods ending in __Action are mapped to endpoints using their method names. Actions can accept no parameters or one string parameter containing the raw query string. Actions must return string. Exceptions thrown by an action result in an HTTP 500 response containing a JSON error object. GetActionResponseText() and GetActionResponseMessage() target the action endpoint matching the calling test method's name. GetControllerResponseText() and GetControllerResponseMessage() send requests to arbitrary application routes. HostStop() stops the application associated with the configured port. Example public class UserTests : BaseTestKestrel { protected int Port = 41021; public string GetUser__Action(string query) { return userService.GetUser(query).Json(); } [TestMethod] public void GetUser() { HostStart(); var response = GetActionResponseMessage("id=1"); Assert.AreEqual(HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode); } } Caveats Each independent test host should use a unique port. Classes using the same port share the same application instance. Action methods must return string and accept either no parameters or one string parameter. Missing action endpoints return HTTP 404 with a message identifying the expected action name. Non-success responses from the request helpers are logged but do not automatically fail the test. outputLogPath on HostStart() is currently only included in the console output; it does not configure file logging.

documentation/basetestserver.html.title: BaseTestServer | System Library Common Framework
documentation/basetestserver.html.summary: BaseTestServer BaseTestServer provides an in-memory ASP.NET Core test host using Microsoft's TestServer. It allows integration testing of controllers and framework middleware without opening a network port. Features In-memory hosting: Runs the ASP.NET application using TestServer. Framework middleware: Initializes the framework services and middleware pipeline. Custom configuration: Supports callbacks for services, application configuration, and logging. HTTP helpers: Sends GET requests and returns either the response body or the complete response message. Rebuild: Recreates the test host when services or middleware need to be reconfigured. Behavior The host and HttpClient are initialized lazily on first access to Client. GetResponseText() returns the response body. Unsuccessful responses are logged but do not throw automatically. GetResponseMessage() returns the complete HttpResponseMessage, allowing tests to inspect the status code, headers, and content. RebuildClient() disposes the current TestServer. The next request initializes a new host and client. Example public class UserTests : BaseTestServer { [TestMethod] public void GetUser() { var response = GetResponseMessage("/api/users?id=1"); Assert.AreEqual(HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode); } } Caveats Requests are sent through the in-memory test host; no real network port is opened. The supplied request helpers use GET. Non-success responses returned by GetResponseText() are logged but do not automatically fail the test.

documentation/cache.html.title: Cache | System Library Common Framework
documentation/cache.html.summary: Cache Application-level in-memory cache with built-in sharding for thread safety and scalability. Features Sharded cache: 8 cache containers out of the box Auto-generated key: includes namespace, class, method name, IsAuthenticated, user roles, and scoped variables of type string, int, DateTime, bool, or enum Behavior Duration: 3 minutes default CacheDuration: Predefined enum or any integer (seconds) Capacity: 320,000 items across 8 shards (40,000 per shard, configurable) Eviction: When full, 33% of items are removed via IMemoryCache eviction policy Fallback [Pro Tier]: Serves previously cached data when getItem() returns null or throws, for up to 3 minutes after primary expiration Skip Options skipWhenAuthenticated: Defaults to false skipWhenAdmin: Defaults to true, matches roles: Admin, Admins, Administrator, Administrators, WebAdmins, CmsAdmins (and lowercase variants) skipWhen: Custom condition, return true to skip Response cache Output cache Cache entire page or controller responses, with skip support for admins and authenticated users: // On a controller action: [OutputCache(Tags = [OutputCacheTag.SkipWhenAdmin])] public IActionResult Index() { ... } // On a razor page: @attribute [OutputCache(Tags = [OutputCacheTag.SkipWhenAdmin])] Available tags: OutputCacheTag.SkipWhenAdmin — skips cache for admin users OutputCacheTag.SkipWhenAuthenticated — skips cache for any authenticated user Warning SkipWhenAuthenticated and SkipWhenAdmin do not work on Razor Pages — controllers only. Caveats Auto-generated key is never user-specific — pass your own key containing userId/email to cache per user null is never cached Cache.Clear() may return default to concurrent callers during the brief reinitalization window Auto-generated key is capped at 2000 characters and 64 scoped variables — exceeding either logs an error Cache.Lock() is not a true lock — concurrent threads can still slip through Tip Pick duration by asking "what is the minimum time this data can be stale?" — always round down to the nearest CacheDuration value. AppSettings View all appsettings here

documentation/client.html.title: Client | System Library Common Framework
documentation/client.html.summary: Client The framework Client wraps outbound HTTP requests and is designed for reuse, resilience, and simplified integration code. Features HTTP verbs: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS, and related requests Connection reuse: underlying HttpClient instances are reused based on host and connection configuration Retry behavior: retries are applied according to the request type and configured policy Fluent usage: call directly from a string URL or a typed client instance Resilience: supports the framework’s default timeout and error-handling behavior Behavior The framework caches HttpClient instances per host, port, timeout, scheme, SSL, and decompression configuration so requests can reuse a healthy connection instead of creating a new client every time. Retry policy disabled (default): Always retries once on 502, 504 for GET, POST and file requests Always retries once if remote host forcibly closes the connection These base retries cannot be disabled Retry policy enabled: All of the above, plus retries on 401, 404, 500 for GET/POST and file requests Up to two retries if response is null (timeout) 666ms delay between retries useRetryPolicy: false (default) Retries once on 502, 504 (GET, POST, file requests) useRetryPolicy: true Same as false, plus: Retries one extra time on 502, 504 (GET, POST) Retries twice if response is null (timeout/no response) Retries once on: 401 for GET, POST 404 for GET 500 for GET, POST 404, 500, 502, 504 for file requests 404, 502, 504 for OPTION, PATCH, HEAD, CONNECT, TRACE** var client = new Client(); var response = client.Get<string>("https://api.example.com/data"); The same pattern also works via URL-based extensions: var response = "https://api.example.com/data".GetRequest<string>(); Caveats DELETE and PUT requests are not retried. throwOnUnsuccessful defaults to false, so some failures are logged rather than thrown. ClientCertificate must include a private key or an exception is raised when used. Retry behavior is intentionally conservative and depends on the framework’s configuration. Tip Inherit from Client to build typed integration clients that share a base URL, headers, and authentication logic across your application. AppSettings View all appsettings here

documentation/config.html.title: Config | System Library Common Framework
documentation/config.html.summary: Config Config<T> is the framework’s typed configuration abstraction for JSON, XML, and .config-style settings. It loads configuration into strongly typed C# objects from files, appsettings.json, or Azure Key Vault. Features Auto-discovery: locates files by class name in ~/, ~/Configs/, and ~/Configurations/. Environment transforms: supports ClassName.Environment.json overrides. Decryption: decrypts encrypted properties using ConfigDecryptAttribute. AppSettings support: loads configuration from named sections in appsettings.json. Environment variables: supports environment-specific overrides. Key Vault support: loads configuration and environment transforms from Azure Key Vault. Behavior Configuration is loaded lazily on first access to T.Current and cached for the lifetime of the application. Files are discovered by class name using case-insensitive matching. Environment-specific transforms are applied on top of the base configuration when available. When Key Vault is configured through systemLibraryCommonFramework:config:keyVaultUrl, the framework can load: {groupName}.json {groupName}.{Environment}.json These are applied as configuration values and environment transforms. Dots in secret names are replaced with hyphens to comply with Key Vault naming restrictions. Environment-variable overrides use the following prefixes: APP_ for configuration files outside appsettings.json. APP_, ASPNETCORE_, and DOTNET_ for appsettings.json. Decryption Properties decorated with ConfigDecryptAttribute are decrypted during configuration loading. public class PokemonConfig : Config<PokemonConfig> { public string Token { get; set; } [ConfigDecrypt("Token")] public string TokenDecrypted { get; set; } } Values must be encrypted using the framework's string.Encrypt() method so the same default key is used during decryption. Example public class PokemonConfig : Config<PokemonConfig> { public string Url { get; set; } public int CacheDuration { get; set; } } var url = PokemonConfig.Current.Url; Example configuration files: PokemonConfig.json PokemonConfig.Production.json PokemonConfig.Development.json Caveats T cannot be a nested type. The configuration file must exist and cannot be empty. Decryption failures throw exceptions. Key Vault retrieval failures are logged as warnings, and startup continues without the unavailable values. Tip Encrypted values can be stored alongside source code, as long as the encryption key is kept separate.

documentation/controllers.html.title: Controllers | System Library Common Framework
documentation/controllers.html.summary: Controllers The framework adds routing conventions and helper behavior on top of ASP.NET MVC. Features Auto-routing: controllers are routed automatically based on class name and namespace BaseApiController: adds JSON and XML response helpers for API actions Action matching: overload resolution prefers the action whose parameters best match the request values Short route aliases: names such as PokemonApiController resolve to both long and short route variants Behavior Controllers inheriting from Controller or BaseApiController are discovered automatically by the framework. The routing conventions apply without requiring [Route] attributes on every controller. API endpoints are built under /api/ and follow the controller/action pattern. Namespace segments beyond the root are included in the route path when present. MyApp.Api.Admin.UserApiController -> /api/admin/userapi/ and /api/admin/user/ The auto-routing logic prefers the action whose parameter names best match the incoming query string values when multiple actions could match the same request. BaseApiController exposes convenience response helpers such as Json(object data, bool camelCase = true) and Xml(object data). Caveats Controllers with explicit [Route] attributes are excluded from the framework’s automatic convention behavior. Controllers marked with [ApiController] are also excluded from the auto-routing pattern. The framework does not replace the ASP.NET routing system; it adds a convention layer and friendly action selection behavior. Tip Inherit BaseApiController for API endpoints when you want the framework to handle response shaping and route conventions for you.

documentation/dispatch.html.title: Dispatch | System Library Common Framework
documentation/dispatch.html.summary: Dispatch Static helpers for running functions in parallel or as fire-and-forget background tasks. Features Dispatch.Parallel<T>(): runs multiple functions in parallel, collects and returns results Dispatch.Parallel(): runs multiple actions in parallel, no return value Dispatch.FireAndForget(): runs actions in background threads — non-blocking, caller never waits Behavior Parallel uses Parallel.ForEach with max degree of parallelism set to ProcessorCount / 4 — intentionally conservative to avoid starving the web server thread pool. Default timeout is 30 seconds — configurable per call. If timeout is hit, collected results so far are returned and an error is logged. Exceptions inside individual functions are caught, logged and skipped — remaining functions continue. FireAndForget wraps each action in Task.Run — each action runs independently on the thread pool. Exceptions are caught and passed to the optional onError callback. If no callback is provided exceptions are silently swallowed. Caveats Parallel result order is not guaranteed — ConcurrentBag is unordered Parallel null return values are silently skipped — default(T) is added on exception FireAndForget actions run until completion or app shutdown — no cancellation support FireAndForget without onError callback swallows all exceptions silently Tip Use Parallel for independent IO calls that can run simultaneously — fetching from multiple APIs, loading multiple config files. Use FireAndForget for work that must not block the caller — sending emails, writing audit logs. !!SKIP!!

documentation/encryption.html.title: Encryption | System Library Common Framework
documentation/encryption.html.summary: Encryption Extension methods for encrypting and decrypting strings and byte arrays using AES CBC, AES GCM, RSA, or the ASP.NET Data Protection key ring. All methods are available directly on string and byte[]. Features AES CBC: symmetric encryption, default algorithm, IV prepended to output AES GCM: symmetric encryption with authentication tag, tamper-evident RSA: asymmetric encryption using auto-generated or custom PEM key files Key Ring: wraps ASP.NET Data Protection API — useful for short-lived tokens and cookies Auto key discovery: key file is located automatically by scanning parent directories — no configuration required in most cases Behavior Key resolution order at startup: CLI argument --slcf-encryption-key=yourkey Environment variable SLCF_ENCRYPTION_KEY Key file named enc-*.key in configured or auto-discovered directory Falls back to default key ABCD... The resolved key is hashed together with 'app:name' to produce a final 32-byte AES key, meaning the same raw key produces different keys across different app names. Key file discovery scans parent directories upward from the app root (up to 10 levels) looking for enc-*.key, pem.pub and pem.priv files. If multiple .key files exist the oldest is used — allowing key rotation without breaking existing encrypted values. RSA key files are auto-generated on first use if none exist in the configured directory. Public key (.pub) is used for encryption, private key (.priv) for decryption. Decryption caching: frequently decrypted short values (under 255 chars) are cached in memory — up to 64 entries per algorithm — to avoid repeated decryption overhead. Key Ring uses the app name as the protection purpose — requires app:name to be set in appsettings in production or it throws. Caveats Default fallback key ABC... is shared across all framework users — never use it in production AES CBC key must be 16, 24 or 32 bytes — throws otherwise AES GCM IV must be 12 bytes, AES CBC IV must be 16 bytes — throws otherwise RSA requires a private key for decryption — throws if private key is missing Key Ring encrypted values cannot be decrypted across applications or after key ring rotation unless persistence is configured Encrypted values in config files may trigger GitHub secret scanning — add config paths to .github/secret_scanning.yml to suppress Tip Store your enc-*.key file outside the repository as the filename after enc- is your encryption password. For stronger keys with unrestricted characters, pass the key via CLI argument --slcf-encryption-key= or environment variable SLCF_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Use minimum 32 characters mixing uppercase, lowercase, digits and symbols as the key — the longer and more random the better. AppSettings View all appsettings here

documentation/enum.html.title: Enum | System Library Common Framework
documentation/enum.html.summary: Enum Extensions and attributes for enriching enums with metadata, enabling conversion between enum keys, custom text and custom values — with full support in JSON serialization. Features EnumTextAttribute for display-friendly enum names EnumValueAttribute for machine-readable values ToText() to convert enum to text ToValue() to convert enum to custom value GetEnumText() to retrieve the attribute value without fallback GetEnumValue() to retrieve the attribute value without fallback ToEnum() to convert strings back to enum values IsAny() to check whether an enum value matches any value in a set EnumExtensions<TEnum> for generic enum helpers ASP.NET model binding support JSON serialization/deserialization support Behavior ToEnum() matching priority: Direct key name match (case insensitive) EnumValue attribute match (case insensitive) EnumText attribute match (case insensitive) Returns first key in enum (default) if no match ToValue() strips leading underscore from keys formatted as _0something — allowing numeric-prefixed enum keys that are invalid in C# without the underscore prefix. JSON serialization via string.Json() respects both EnumValue and EnumText attributes during deserialization and serialization. TypeDescriptor — all ASP.NET model binding automatically uses EnumValue and EnumText attribute matching when converting strings to enums, including query strings, form posts and route values. Caveats GetEnumText() and GetEnumValue() return null if attribute is not present — use ToText() / ToValue() if you want a fallback to key name EnumExtensions<T> uses static methods instead of extension methods due to C# generic type constraints Tip Use EnumValue for machine-readable identifiers (IDs, codes, symbols) and EnumText for human-readable display strings — they serve different purposes and can both be applied to the same key. Examples public enum Status { [EnumText("Open")] Open, [EnumValue("in_progress")] InProgress, [EnumText("Closed")] [EnumValue("closed")] Closed } Status.Open.ToText(); // "Open" Status.InProgress.ToValue(); // "in_progress" Status.InProgress.GetEnumValue(); // "in_progress" Status.Closed.GetEnumText(); // "Closed" ASP.NET model binding public IActionResult Get([FromQuery] Status status) { return Ok(status); } Requests with query params such as these bind correctly: ?status=Open ?status=in_progress ?status=Closed JSON serialization var json = new { status = Status.InProgress }.Json(); This serializes using the configured enum value instead of the raw numeric underlying enum value. Example with numeric-like enum names public enum Codes { _0, _1, _2A } Codes._1.ToValue(); // "1" Generic enum helpers var keys = EnumExtensions<Color>.GetKeys(); var values = EnumExtensions<Color>.GetValues(); var enums = EnumExtensions<Color>.GetEnums();

documentation/environmentinfo.html.title: EnvironmentInfo | System Library Common Framework
documentation/environmentinfo.html.summary: EnvironmentInfo EnvironmentInfo provides global metadata about the application's current runtime environment without requiring dependency injection. Features Environment name: EnvironmentInfo.Name preserves the original ASP.NET Core environment name, including casing. Environment type: EnvironmentInfo.Type maps the environment name to the framework's EnvironmentType enum. Development flag: EnvironmentInfo.IsDev Test flag: EnvironmentInfo.IsTest Automation flag: EnvironmentInfo.IsAutomation Production flag: EnvironmentInfo.IsProd Global access: static properties are available throughout the application. Behavior EnvironmentInfo initializes once when first accessed, reading the environment name from ASP.NET Core and mapping it to EnvironmentType. Caveats If the environment name does not match a defined EnvironmentType, the type defaults to Development.

documentation/extensions.html.title: Extensions | System Library Common Framework
documentation/extensions.html.summary: Extensions A lof of common extensions for any application, heres a sample list of the most useful ones: Features StringExtensions: Is() and IsNot() ToDateTime() ToDate() ToMd5() ToBase64() and FromBase64() Compress() and Decompress() Obfuscate() and Unobfuscate() ToPascalCase() and toCamelCase() MaxLength() GetSampledKey() GetFingerprint() Encrypt() and Decrypt() ConcurrentDictionaryExtensions: Cache() StringBuilderExtensions: Is() and IsNot() IndexOf() EndsWith() GetSampledKey() GetFingerprint() IListExtensions: Is() and IsNot() Behavior All extension methods should work out of the box and most never throws.

documentation/frameworkoptions.html.title: FrameworkOptions | System Library Common Framework
documentation/frameworkoptions.html.summary: FrameworkOptions Controls which services and middleware are registered at startup. Passed to Application.Start, Application.Build or the extension API. Features All options default to sensible values — only override what you need. Middleware toggles: UseAuthentication — default true UseAuthorization — default true UseForwardedHeaders — default true UseHttpsRedirection — default false UseHsts — default false UseOutputCache — default true UseGzipResponseCompression — default true UseBrotliResponseCompression — default false UseDeveloperPage — default true UseStatusCodeLogger — default true UseStaticFilePolicy — default true UseSecurityPolicy — default true UseResponseCaching — default true UseDataProtectionPolicy — default false Static files: StaticFilesClientCacheSeconds — default 604800 (7 days) StaticRequestPaths — custom static file root paths Views: ViewLocations — custom view location formats ViewLocationExpander — custom IViewLocationExpander implementation ApplicationParts — additional assemblies scanned for controllers Behavior UseSecurityPolicy only adds security headers in production — non-production environments allow all content freely to simplify local development and testing. UseDataProtectionPolicy generates a single key file in the parent of ContentRoot valid for 100 years — copy it to all environments and gitignore it. Required for EncryptUsingKeyRing and DecryptUsingKeyRing and for cookie encryption across multiple instances. Caveats UseDataProtectionPolicy is false by default — keys are stored in-memory only, meaning auth cookies are lost on app restart and won't work across multiple instances. Enable it to persist keys to disk. UseHsts and UseHttpsRedirection are both false by default — enable only if your hosting environment does not handle HTTPS termination upstream StaticRequestPaths requires UseStaticFilePolicy to be true Tip Enable UseDataProtectionPolicy in production if you use cookie authentication or run multiple instances — otherwise users will be logged out on every restart. Copy the generated key file to all environments and gitignore it. Usage var options = new FrameworkOptions(); Application.Start<Hooks>(AppType.Web, options, AppHosting.Kestrel);

documentation/hooks.html.title: Hooks | System Library Common Framework
documentation/hooks.html.summary: Hooks Callbacks for hooking into framework startup — register services, extend the middleware pipeline and react to host events. Features Service registration: OnConfigureServices — register your own services alongside framework services Pipeline hooks: tap into the request pipeline at specific points Host lifecycle hooks: react to host building, built and started events Behavior Service hook: OnConfigureServices(services, env) → called during service registration Pipeline hooks (called per branch — Web, Static, Api): OnPipelineBegin → after rate limiter and block middleware, before all others OnBeforeEndpoints → called before controllers and routes are mapped OnAfterEndpoints → called after controllers and routes are mapped — add extra endpoints here OnPipelineEnd → after pipeline is fully built Host lifecycle hooks: OnHostBuilding → configure host (logging, DI, etc.) OnHostBuilt → read final host configuration OnHostStarted → app is live — perform warmup, seed data, start background jobs Caveats All hook methods have default empty implementations — only override what you need IFrameworkHooks is not invoked when using the Framework Extension API — use extension methods directly in that case OnAuthorization requires both UseAuthentication and UseAuthorization to be true in FrameworkOptions Tip Use OnHostStarted for warmup tasks like pre-loading cache or seeding data — the host is fully live at that point and all services are available.

documentation/httpcontextinstance.html.title: HttpContextInstance | System Library Common Framework
documentation/httpcontextinstance.html.summary: HttpContextInstance Global access to the current HttpContext without having to inject it through a dependency chain. Features Current context accessor: HttpContextInstance.Current returns the active request context from anywhere in the app Static helper support: useful in extension methods and framework-level utilities that do not accept a HttpContext parameter Behavior var context = HttpContextInstance.Current; var path = context.Request?.Path; When no HTTP request is active, the framework returns a default empty context instead of null, which makes static helpers safe to call during background work, testing, or console execution. Caveats If no HTTP request is active, the returned object is a default empty HttpContext with an empty ClaimsPrincipal. This is intended for code paths that need a safe default, not for forcing a real request context. AddFrameworkServices() should be called during startup so that the singleton access pattern is registered correctly. Tip Use HttpContextInstance.Current in static helpers where you need request data but do not want to pass HttpContext through every method call.

documentation/index.html.title: Docs | System Library Common Framework
documentation/index.html.summary: Docs This section contains the detailed technical documentation for the framework modules. Each document explains how a feature works, what it is intended to do, where it is useful, and what to watch out for. Table of contents !!TOC!!

documentation/json.html.title: Json | System Library Common Framework
documentation/json.html.summary: Json The framework extends JSON handling with helper methods and serializer support for common runtime types. Features object.Json(): serialize to a JSON string string.Json<T>(): deserialize a JSON payload into a known type string.JsonFind<T>(): navigate a nested payload and extract a specific value by path Attribute-based transformations: encryption, obfuscation, and compression can be applied transparently during serialization Behavior The framework includes converter support for common values such as string, int, long, DateTime, DateTimeOffset, Guid, Uri, and enums. Non-serializable types such as Exception, Thread, and Stream are skipped rather than crashing the serializer. var json = myObject.Json(); var model = json.Json<MyType>(); JsonFind<T>() is especially useful when consuming larger third-party payloads and you need only a small subset of the data. Caveats JsonFind<T>() throws when the selected path does not exist. dynamic payloads bypass some of the framework’s converter behavior, so values may come back as raw strings. JsonSerializerOptions are rebuilt per call, which preserves thread safety without relying on a shared static serializer instance. Tip Use JsonFind<T>() when you need a single value from a larger document without deserializing the full payload tree.

documentation/log.html.title: Log | System Library Common Framework
documentation/log.html.summary: Log The framework exposes a global Log type for application logging without dependency injection. Features Global access: Log.Error(), Log.Warning(), Log.Information(), Log.Debug(), Log.Trace(), and Log.Dump() Background queueing: messages are queued and flushed on a background thread instead of blocking the calling thread Custom output: supports file output, stdout/stderr, and custom ILogWriter implementations Enrichment: can attach request and user context when available Behavior Log writes are checked against the configured minimum log level before being queued. Log.Dump() is the direct-write debug helper for cases where immediate output is more useful than queueing. Log.Warning("Retrying request"); Log.Dump("diagnostic payload"); The framework can also forward logs to stdout/stderr or consume stdout/stderr with an ILogWriter implementation when configured through the framework logging pipeline. Caveats Log.Dump() bypasses some of the normal queue and filter behavior and is meant for diagnostics, not production logging. File logging is a fallback behavior; custom sinks are preferred in production systems. Logging is not a substitute for structured observability systems such as Application Insights, Datadog, or OpenTelemetry. Tip Implement ILogWriter and register it as a singleton to route messages to your preferred sink while keeping the framework’s formatting and enrichment behavior consistent. AppSettings View all appsettings here

documentation/metrics.html.title: Metrics | System Library Common Framework
documentation/metrics.html.summary: Metrics Prometheus-based metrics with a built-in pie chart UI. Increment counters anywhere in your code and view them as charts at a dedicated endpoint — no external tools required. Features Metric.Inc(label, segment): increment a counter from anywhere in code Built-in UI: pie charts rendered at /metrics/ui Multi-node support: UI fetches metrics from all running instances simultaneously Auto-coloring: segment names like error, success, timeout get meaningful colors automatically Custom colors and ordering: configure per-metric via MetricCharts Behavior Two endpoints are registered automatically when metrics are enabled: /metrics → raw Prometheus text format /metrics/ui → pie chart dashboard (Pro Tier) UI is cached for 20 seconds — refreshes automatically on next request after expiry. Multi-node fetching makes 7 parallel requests to the metrics endpoint — aggregates results across load balanced instances. Auto-color mapping based on segment name: error, fail, crash, 500, 502 → red success, hit, ok, 200, 201 → green warn, notfound, 404 → orange timeout, unauthorized, 401 → light red circuit, broken, 503 → dark red Caveats Metrics UI requires Pro Tier license Metric.Inc() is a no-op if metrics are disabled — zero overhead Multi-node fetching assumes all instances are reachable on the same host/port — configure metricUIUrl in appsettings if behind a proxy Default Prometheus metrics are suppressed — only framework and consumer metrics are shown Tip Use label for the category and segment for the outcome: Metric.Inc("checkout", "success"); Metric.Inc("checkout", "timeout"); Metric.Inc("cache", "hit"); Metric.Inc("cache","miss"); Most common segments are auto-colored — success is green, timeout is red, no configuration needed. AppSettings View all appsettings here

documentation/security.html.title: Security | System Library Common Framework
documentation/security.html.summary: Security The framework adds a baseline of security behaviors out of the box — not a substitute for proper security testing, but a reasonable starting point. Features Request blocking: Requests to sensitive paths and file extensions are blocked automatically — see Static Files for the full list. Security headers (production only): X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — all responses Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=2592000; includeSubDomains — always sent, browsers respect it only over HTTPS Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin — on non-file requests Content-Security-Policy — web responses only: All sources allowed (default-src *) Plugin embedding blocked (object-src 'none') Base URI restricted to same origin (base-uri 'self') Iframing restricted to your domain and subdomains (frame-ancestors) Bot and crawler blocking: UserAgentFilter attribute blocks known bots and crawlers when applied to a controller or action. Encryption: AES CBC, AES GCM and RSA available out of the box — see Encryption. What the framework does NOT do Penetration testing Vulnerability scanning OWASP compliance verification Security auditing Whitelist or validate scripts running on your site as CSP is set to default-src * Caveats Security headers are only added in production — other environments allow all content freely to simplify local development and testing TODO: And should also be added to preproduction - so we have an environment equal to production

documentation/services.html.title: Services | System Library Common Framework
documentation/services.html.summary: Services Global service locator providing access to the configured IServiceProvider anywhere in the application — without injection. Features Services.Get<T>(): resolve any registered service globally Behavior var accessor = Services.Get<IHttpContextAccessor>(); var context = accessor?.HttpContext; Services.Current is initialized twice: At bootstrap with a minimal default provider (HttpContextAccessor, DataProtection, etc.) Overwritten when UseFrameworkBeginMiddleware is invoked This ensures framework internals work even before the full DI container is available. Caveats Returns null if service is not registered — no exception thrown Avoid using Services.Get<T>() in constructors during startup — the full provider may not be initialized yet This is a service locator — use constructor injection where possible, reserve this for places where injection is not available (static classes, extension methods, filters) Tip Use Services.Get<T>() in static contexts where DI injection is not possible — global helpers, static extensions, or framework internals. For regular classes prefer constructor injection.

documentation/shardeddicstionary.html.title: ShardedDictionary | System Library Common Framework
documentation/shardeddicstionary.html.summary: ShardedDictionary A thread-safe generic dictionary that distributes keys across 4 shards to reduce lock contention and improve throughput under concurrent load. Features Sharded storage: 4 internal ConcurrentDictionary shards — keys distributed by hash Auto-clear: each shard clears itself when it reaches capacity — no manual management needed Cache helper: Cache(key, getItem) returns existing value or creates and stores a new one Standard API: TryAdd, TryGetValue, TryRemove, ContainsKey, TryUpdate, Clear, Count, Keys Behavior Shard is selected by key.GetHashCode() & 3 — O(1) shard lookup. When a shard exceeds its capacity (maxItemCount / 4), the entire shard is cleared before adding the new item. This is a hard clear — not LRU, not eviction — all items in that shard are lost. Default total capacity is 100,000 items (25,000 per shard). Cache() is a get-or-create helper — if key exists returns it, otherwise calls getItem(), stores and returns result. Used extensively inside the framework for reflection caching. Caveats Shard clear is all-or-nothing — when capacity is hit, entire shard is wiped, not just oldest entries Count property iterates all 4 shards — slightly expensive, avoid in tight loops Keys property yields across all shards — not a snapshot, concurrent modifications may affect iteration ClearLock is a static object — shared across ALL ShardedDictionary instances, potential contention Tip Use Cache() instead of TryGetValue + TryAdd — it handles the get-or-create pattern atomically per shard.

documentation/staticfiles.html.title: StaticFiles | System Library Common Framework
documentation/staticfiles.html.summary: StaticFiles Serves static files from well-known asset folders with sensible defaults — cache headers, compression and unknown file type support out of the box. Features Auto-discovery: serves files from wwwroot, public, static, dist, frontend, assets, files automatically Client-side caching: Cache-Control: public, max-age=604800, immutable applied to all static files by default (7 days) Unknown file types: served without restriction — no file extension whitelist Compression: HTTPS compression enabled by default Behavior Static files are served from two sources: WebRootPath (wwwroot) — standard ASP.NET web root, served at / Asset folders — served at their folder name as path segment: ~/public/ → /public/ ~/static/ → /static/ ~/dist/ → /dist/ ~/frontend/ → /frontend/ ~/assets/ → /assets/ ~/files/ → /files/ Only GET and HEAD requests are handled — all other methods pass through to the next middleware. Cache header is only added if not already present — consumers can override per file or route. Security Certain paths and file extensions are blocked automatically — returns 403 Forbidden: Blocked paths: /app_data/ /properties/ /configs/ /configurations/ /bin/ /obj/ appsettings.* Blocked extensions: .exe .dll .iso .msi .ps1 .cmd .sh .bash .vbs .dmg .config .env .ini .key .pem .cshtml .cs .sql .mdf .bat .jar .php .py .pl .rb .go .vb .hta .bak .db .pfx .crt This runs before static file serving — blocked requests never reach the file system. Caveats UseStaticFilePolicy must be true in FrameworkOptions — enabled by default If WebRootPath is set but folder does not exist — logs a warning and continues Cache duration is controlled by StaticFilesClientCacheSeconds in FrameworkOptions — default 604800 (7 days) Tip Place your CSS, JS and images in ~/wwwroot or any of the auto-discovered asset folders — no configuration needed. Files are immediately available at their path.

documentation/systemtype.html.title: SystemType | System Library Common Framework
documentation/systemtype.html.summary: SystemType Static class providing pre-cached Type instances for common .NET types. Avoids repeated typeof() calls throughout the framework and in consumer code. Features Covers all common types: Primitives: string, int, long, short, bool, char, byte, double, decimal, float, uint, ulong, ushort Dates: DateTime, DateTimeOffset, TimeSpan — including nullable variants Collections: IList, ICollection, IDictionary, List<>, Dictionary<,> — generic and non-generic Other: Guid, Uri, object, ExpandoObject, Delegate, Tuple, BigInteger, Half Attributes: EnumValueAttribute, EnumTextAttribute Arrays: byte[], int[] Behavior All fields are static and initialized once at class load — zero overhead after first access. Caveats Fields are public static not readonly — technically mutable, but should never be reassigned Tip Use SystemType.IntType instead of typeof(int) in hot paths — the cached instance avoids repeated type resolution overhead. Particularly useful in reflection-heavy code called frequently. Usage if(type == SystemType.IntType) { ... }

documentation/views.html.title: Views | System Library Common Framework
documentation/views.html.summary: Views The framework extends ASP.NET view discovery so controllers and their views can live together in feature-style folders. Features Feature-folder support: views are discovered beside their controllers Namespace discovery: controller namespaces are added as view search roots Custom locations: additional view paths can be supplied through FrameworkOptions.ViewLocations Custom expander support: a custom IViewLocationExpander can be added alongside the built-in behavior Behavior The framework registers several built-in view search paths automatically: /{controller}/{view}.cshtml /{namespaceSegment}/{controller}/{view}.cshtml /{namespaceSegment}/{controller}/{controller}.cshtml /{namespaceSegment}/{controller}/Views/{view}.cshtml /{namespaceSegment}/Views/Shared/{controller}/{view}.cshtml When the framework discovers a controller namespace, it also registers that namespace segment as a valid view root. This makes folder-based features easy to structure without manually wiring view locations. Caveats Built-in view paths take priority over custom view paths. View namespace discovery happens as controller metadata is discovered, not during a global startup pass. If controllers live in external assemblies, ApplicationParts configuration may still be needed. The custom ViewLocationExpander runs alongside the built-in expander; both are active. Tip Keep a controller and its matching view in the same feature folder to align with the framework’s default conventions and avoid extra configuration.

tutorial/index.html.title: Tutorial | System Library Common Framework
tutorial/index.html.summary:
Tutorial Duration: 30 minutes This tutorial guides you through the framework’s common startup and module patterns: configuration, logging, controllers, static files, API controllers, and caching. Prerequisite Follow the installation steps for the project. Ensure your app has an appsettings.json file with an application name: { "systemLibraryCommonFramework": { "app": { "name": "company_unique_appname" } } } Chapter 1: Startup The framework supports several startup approaches. The most flexible pattern is the direct host-builder extension API. Extension API Program.cs - fill in code: using SystemLibrary.Common.Framework; using SystemLibrary.Common.Framework.App; using SystemLibrary.Common.Framework.App.Extensions; using SystemLibrary.Common.Framework.Extensions; var options = new FrameworkOptions(); var builder = Host.CreateDefaultBuilder(args); builder.ConfigureFrameworkLogging(); builder.ConfigureServices((context, services) => { services = services.AddFrameworkServices(AppType.Web, options); }); builder = builder.ConfigureWebHostDefaults(webBuilder => { webBuilder.ConfigureFrameworkHosting(); webBuilder.Configure(app => { app.UseFrameworkBeginMiddlewares(AppType.Web); app.UseFrameworkEndMiddlewares(AppType.Web); }); }); var app = builder.Build(); app.Run(); The framework also exposes Application.Start(...) and Application.Start(...) helpers when you want the framework to manage the full host lifecycle for you. Chapter 2: Configuration The framework provides typed configuration through Config. The config is loaded from files that match the type name and is cached after the first access. Create configurations ~/Configs/PokemonConfig.json { "url": "https://localhost:5010/api", "cacheDuration": 10 } ~/Configs/PokemonConfig.Development.json { "url": "https://localhost:5010/api", "cacheDuration": 4 } ~/Configs/PokemonConfig.cs public class PokemonConfig : Config { public string Url { get; set; } public int CacheDuration { get; set; } } Chapter 3: Controllers and views Controllers can live alongside their views in feature folders and the framework will discover those paths automatically. Create: ~/Content/Home/HomeController.cs public class HomeController : Controller { public IActionResult Index() { Log.Information("Home requested"); return View(); } } ~/Content/Home/Index.cshtml @model object

Home

The Home page is available at: http://localhost:5010/ http://localhost:5010/Home The Home controller is registered as the default homepage, so an empty Path routes to its Index action. Chapter 4: Static files Asset folders such as wwwroot, public, static, dist, frontend, assets, and files are served automatically. Example, create an asset folder and place an image: ~/wwwroot/image.png Then it is served as: http://localhost:5010/image.png Chapter 5: API controllers API controllers inherit from BaseApiController, which adds JSON/XML response helpers. public class PokemonApiController : BaseApiController { public IActionResult Pikachu() { return Json(new { name = "Pikachu" }); } } The framework adds route conventions and action matching based on controller names and namespaces. Chapter 6: The client Use the framework Client to execute outbound HTTP calls while reusing connection state and applying the framework’s retry behavior. var client = new Client(); var response = client.Get(PokemonConfig.Current.Url + "/pokemon/pikachu"); Chapter 7: Cache The framework cache is sharded and supports auto-generated keys, auth/admin skip rules, and conditional cache entries. var name = Cache.Get("pokemon-pikachu", () => { var client = new Client(); var response = client.Get(PokemonConfig.Current.Url + "/pokemon/pikachu"); return response.Data?.name; }, CacheDuration.M); The generated key includes the calling context and user state when no explicit key is passed. Chapter 8: More modules The framework includes additional modules for encryption, JSON, metrics, assemblies, and method helpers. See the documentation section for each module for deeper details.
